lessons.title: Prefixes 小- and 第-
lessons.summary: 小- makes a friendly or young form of a name or noun; 第- makes an ordinal number.
body: A prefix attaches to the front of a word. 小 (xiǎo) before a surname or a noun makes a friendly, often younger form: 小王, 小朋友, 小学生. 第 (dì) before a number makes an ordinal: 第一 (first), 第二 (second).
The contrast example uses the suffix 们, which attaches to the back of a word (同学们). Prefixes go in front, suffixes go behind; both are bound forms, not free words.

examples.reading: Xiǎo Wáng shì wǒ de tóngxué.
zhè shì wǒ de dì-yī běn shū.

lessons.title: Suffixes -们 and -边
lessons.summary: -们 makes a plural for people; -边 turns a position word into a place word.
pattern: 上 / 下 / 里 / 外 / 前 / 后 + 边
body: A suffix attaches to the back of a word. 们 (men) makes pronouns and person-nouns plural: 我们, 你们, 他们, 同学们, 老师们. It is not used after a number (say 三个学生, not 三个学生们).
边 (bian) attaches to a position word to make a place word: 上边, 下边, 里边, 外边, 前边, 后边. The contrast example uses the prefix 小-, which goes in front (小学生); suffixes go behind.

examples.translation: The book is on top of the table.

examples.reading: xuéxiào wàibian yǒu yí ge shāngdiàn.
examples.translation: There is a shop outside the school.
My younger sister is a primary-school pupil.

lessons.title: Position nouns: 上 下 里 外 前 后
lessons.summary: Attach a position word to a noun to say where something is.
pattern: noun + 上 / 下 / 里 / 外 / 前 / 后
body: 上 (shàng, on), 下 (xià, under), 里 (lǐ, in), 外 (wài, outside), 前 (qián, front) and 后 (hòu, back) attach to a noun to make a place phrase: 桌子上, 椅子下, 家里, 学校外边, 前边, 后边. With 在 they say where someone or something is: 书在桌子上.
The contrast example uses 在, the word that introduces the place phrase. Without 在, 我学校 is not a sentence; 在 links the subject to the place (我在学校).

examples.translation: The book is on the table.
The cat is under the chair.
It is cold outside the school.
There is a bookshop in front.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: 会 能 想 要 可以
lessons.summary: Put a modal before the verb to say ability, wish, need or permission.
pattern: subject + 会 / 能 / 想 / 要 / 可以 + verb
body: 会 (huì) is a learned skill (我会说汉语); 能 (néng) is ability or possibility (他能吃十个饺子); 想 (xiǎng) is a wish (我想去中国); 要 (yào) is a need or want, and can take a thing directly (我要一杯茶); 可以 (kěyǐ) is permission (你可以坐出租车).
To negate a modal, put 不 before it: 不想, 不会, 不能. The contrast example shows this. 没 does not negate 会 or 能 (you cannot say 没会开车); 没 negates 有 and past events.

examples.translation: I would like a cup of tea.
I want to go to China.

examples.reading: tā néng chī shí ge jiǎozi.

lessons.title: Separable verbs: 看病 睡觉 说话 上课 上班…
lessons.summary: These verbs already contain an object, so they cannot take another one.
pattern: verb + object inside one word: 睡 + 觉, 看 + 病, 上 + 班
body: 看病, 睡觉, 说话, 上课, 下课, 上班, 下班 and 生病 are verb-plus-object compounds: 睡 (sleep) + 觉, 看 (see) + 病 (illness), 上 (go to) + 班 (work). Because the object is already inside, they cannot take another object or a duration after the whole word.
Put a duration or 了 inside: 睡了八个小时 (not 睡觉了八个小时), 上了课, 看了病. To add an object, use the plain verb: 看医生, not 看病医生. The contrast example shows the plain verb 看 taking the object 医生.

examples.translation: Dad is going to work today.

examples.reading: wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí.

examples.translation: Mum goes to the hospital to see a doctor.
I am going to see a doctor.

lessons.title: Question words: 什么 谁 哪 几 多少 怎么…
lessons.summary: Ask with a question word in the position of the answer; the word order does not change.
pattern: … + 什么 / 谁 / 哪 / 几 / 多少 / 怎么 / 哪儿 + …？
body: 什么 (what), 谁 (who), 哪 (which), 哪儿 / 哪里 (where), 哪些 (which ones), 几 (how many, small), 多少 (how many, any), 多 (how, before an adjective: 多大), 怎么 (how) and 怎么样 (how about) ask for a specific answer. The question word stays where the answer would go: 你叫什么名字？

几 is for small numbers and needs a measure word (几口人); 多少 is for any number (多少钱). The contrast example uses 吗, which makes a yes-no question instead; do not add 吗 to a question that already has a question word (you cannot say 你叫什么吗？).

examples.reading: nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
examples.translation: How many people are there in your family?
How do we get to school?

lessons.title: Personal pronouns: 我 你 您 他 她 它 大家…
lessons.summary: Pronouns stand for people and things; 您 is polite, 它 is for things, 大家 addresses everyone.
pattern: 我 / 你 / 您 / 他 / 她 / 它 (+ 们)
body: 我 (I), 你 (you), 您 (you, polite), 他 (he), 她 (she), 它 (it) and their plurals with 们 (我们, 你们, 他们, 她们, 它们) stand for people and things. 您 shows respect (to a teacher or an older person). 它 is for things and animals. 大家 means everyone.

A singular pronoun cannot be summed up by 都: say 我们都去, not 我都去. The contrast example uses the suffix 们, which makes the plural (同学们); a number already gives the plural, so do not add 们 after it (三个学生, not 三个学生们).

examples.reading: wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo, tā hěn piàoliang.
examples.translation: I have a cat; it is pretty.

examples.text: 我姐姐是医生，她在医院工作。
examples.reading: wǒ jiějie shì yīshēng, tā zài yīyuàn gōngzuò.
examples.translation: My older sister is a doctor; she works in a hospital.

lessons.title: Demonstratives: 这 那 这儿 这些 有的…
lessons.summary: Point near (这) or far (那); 这儿/那儿 are places, 这些/那些 plural, 有的/有些 mean some.
pattern: 这 / 那 (+ 个 / 些 / 儿 / 里)
body: 这 (zhè, this) points near, 那 (nà, that) points far. 这儿 / 这里 and 那儿 / 那里 are places; 这个 / 那个 and 这些 / 那些 point to one or several things; 有的 and 有些 mean some (有的学生). A measure word usually follows 这 / 那 before a noun: 这本书, 那个电影.
The contrast example uses the question word 哪 (which), which asks rather than points and also needs a measure word (哪本书). 这 / 那 point; 哪 asks.

examples.reading: nǐ yào mǎi nǎ běn shū?
examples.translation: Which book do you want to buy?

lessons.title: Numerals: 一 二/两 三…十 百 千 半 零
lessons.summary: Count with numerals; use 两 (not 二) before a measure word, and 半 for half.
body: 一, 二, 三, 四, 五, 六, 七, 八, 九, 十, 百, 千 and 零 are the numerals. Before a measure word, two is 两, not 二: 两个人, 两本书. 二 is used inside numbers: 十二, 二十. 半 (bàn) means half: 半个苹果, 两点半. 零 marks an empty digit.
The contrast example uses the prefix 第, which makes an ordinal (第一 = first), not a count. 一 is read yī when counting or in an ordinal, yí before a fourth tone and yì before other tones.

examples.reading: wǒ chī le bàn ge píngguǒ.

examples.translation: This phone costs a thousand yuan.

examples.reading: wǒ yì tiān chī sān ge píngguǒ.
examples.translation: I eat three apples a day.

examples.reading: tā shì wǒ de dì-yī ge péngyou.

lessons.title: Measure words: 本 个 家 口 块 件 只 元 杯
lessons.summary: A number or 这/那 needs a measure word before the noun; each noun takes its own.
pattern: numeral / 这 / 那 + measure word + noun
body: Between a number (or 这, 那, 几) and a noun, Chinese needs a measure word: 本 for books (一本书), 个 the general one (一个人), 家 for shops and families (两家饭店), 口 for family members (三口人), 块 for money and pieces (二十块), 件 for clothes and matters (一件衣服), 只 for animals (一只猫), 元 for money (formal). 杯 is borrowed from 杯子 for cups of drink (一杯茶).
The contrast example shows 两 before a measure word: before a measure word, two is 两, not 二 (两本书, not 二本书).

examples.reading: tā jiā yǒu sān zhī māo.
wǒ jiā yǒu sān kǒu rén.
examples.translation: There are three people in my family.
This piece of clothing is pretty.

examples.reading: wǒ hē le yì bēi chá.
examples.translation: I drank a cup of tea.

lessons.title: Time measure words: 日 号 岁 点 分 年 天
lessons.summary: Count dates, ages, clock time and durations with time measure words.
pattern: numeral + 岁 / 点 / 分 / 年 / 天 / 号 / 日
body: 岁 (suì) counts age (五岁); 号 and 日 name the day of the month (三月五号 / 三月五日); 点 and 分 tell the clock (八点, 八点十分); 年 and 天 count duration (一年, 三天). After a number, 年 and 天 need no extra measure word, but 月 takes 个 (三个月).
The contrast example uses 半 (half): 八点半 is half past eight, 半小时 is half an hour. 半 is a numeral, not a measure word.

examples.translation: Today is the fifth of March.

examples.reading: wǒ xué le yì nián Hànyǔ.
examples.translation: I have studied Chinese for a year.

examples.reading: wǒ yì tiān gōngzuò bā ge xiǎoshí.
examples.translation: I work eight hours a day.

lessons.title: Degree adverbs: 非常 很 太 真 有点儿
lessons.summary: Put a degree adverb before an adjective; 太…了 exclamates, 有点儿 often signals a complaint.
pattern: subject + 非常 / 很 / 太 / 真 / 有点儿 + adjective
body: 非常 (fēicháng, very), 很 (hěn, very), 太 (tài, too), 真 (zhēn, really) and 有点儿 (yǒudiǎnr, a bit) go before an adjective: 非常热, 很好, 太贵了, 真好, 有点儿忙. 太 usually pairs with 了 to exclaim. 有点儿 often marks something unwanted.

The contrast example uses 一点儿, which measures a quantity of a thing (喝一点儿水) or follows a verb; it does not go before an adjective (you cannot say 一点儿忙). 有点儿 goes before an adjective; 一点儿 goes with a noun.

examples.translation: I would like to drink a little water.

lessons.title: 都: all, both
lessons.summary: 都 sums up the plural subject or the object placed before it; it comes before the verb.
body: 都 (dōu, all, both) sums up what comes before it: a plural subject (我们都去) or an object moved to the front (这些书我都看了). It stands after the subject and before the verb, never at the end.
The contrast example uses 也 (also), which adds one more rather than summing up all. With a singular subject, 都 is wrong (他都很忙 is not said); 也 is fine (他也很忙). When both appear, 也 comes first: 我们也都去.

examples.reading: zhèxiē shū wǒ dōu kàn le.
examples.translation: I have read all these books.

lessons.title: 在 and 正在: action in progress
lessons.summary: Put 在 or 正在 before the verb to say an action is happening now.
body: 在 (zài) and 正在 (zhèngzài) before a verb mark an action in progress: 我在吃饭, 妈妈正在做饭. 正在 stresses right now. This 在 is an adverb, different from the 在 that says where someone is (我在家).
The contrast example uses sentence-final 呢, which also marks an ongoing action (我吃饭呢) and can stand without 在. 了 marks a completed action, not an ongoing one.

lessons.title: 再: again, once more
lessons.summary: 再 before a verb says an action will happen again; it is for future repeats.
body: 再 (zài, again) before a verb says the action will repeat: 请再说一下, 我明天再来. It is used for future or intended repeats, not for a state that continues.

The contrast example uses 还 (still, more), which says a state continues or something is added (我还想买一本书). 再 does not go before a stative verb like 想 (you cannot say 再想买); 还 does. Do not confuse 再 with 在, which marks an action in progress.

examples.reading: nǐ zài chī yí ge bāozi ba.
wǒmen zài kàn yí ge diànyǐng.
wǒ hái xiǎng mǎi yì běn shū.
examples.translation: I still want to buy a book.

lessons.title: 还 and 也: also, still, more
lessons.summary: 也 adds (also); 还 adds more or says still; both come before the verb.
body: 也 (yě, also) adds one more of the same: 我也喜欢猫. 还 (hái, still, more) says a state continues or something is added: 他还有一个妹妹, 我还想喝茶. Both stand after the subject and before the verb.

The contrast example uses 都 (all), which sums up every member rather than adding one. When 也 and 都 appear together, 也 comes first: 我们也都想去. Do not put 也 or 还 after the verb or at the end of the sentence.

examples.reading: tā hái yǒu yí ge mèimei.
examples.translation: He also has a younger sister.
We all want to go too.

examples.text: 苹果很好吃，饺子也很好吃。
examples.reading: píngguǒ hěn hǎochī, jiǎozi yě hěn hǎochī.
examples.translation: Apples are tasty, and dumplings are tasty too.

lessons.title: Negation: 不 没(有) 不要
lessons.summary: 不 negates verbs and adjectives; 没(有) negates 有 and past events; 不要 forbids.
body: 不 (bù) negates a verb or adjective (我不喝茶, 今天不冷); before a fourth tone it is said bú (不是 bú shì). 没 / 没有 (méi / méiyǒu) negates 有 (我没有手机) and says a past event did not happen (昨天我没去学校). 不要 (bú yào) forbids: 请不要说话.
For a past event use 没, not 不, and drop 了 (我没吃饭, not 没吃了饭). The contrast example uses sentence-final 了 with 不 to mark a change of plan: 我不去了 (I am not going anymore). After 没 there is no 了.

examples.translation: I will not drink tea tomorrow.
I did not go to school yesterday.
He does not have a phone.
I do not want to go to work today.

lessons.title: 在: introducing time and place
lessons.summary: 在 + place comes before the verb to say where an action happens; time words also come before the verb.
body: The preposition 在 (zài) introduces a place before the verb: 我在家吃饭, 他在学校学习. A time word also comes before the verb: 我上午在医院看病. The place and time go before the action, not after it.
The contrast example uses the adverb 正在, which marks an action in progress (妈妈正在做饭), not a place. 在 can also be the verb to be at (我在家); here it is a preposition introducing where the action happens.

examples.translation: We have dinner at a restaurant.

examples.reading: wǒ shàngwǔ zài yīyuàn kàn bìng.
examples.translation: I see a doctor at the hospital in the morning.

lessons.title: Prepositions 和 and 对: introducing a person
lessons.summary: 和 introduces a companion (with); 对 introduces the target of an attitude (toward).
body: The preposition 和 (hé, with) introduces a companion before the verb: 我和他一起去学校. 对 (duì, toward) introduces the target of an attitude: 妈妈对我很好. Both come before the verb or adjective.

The contrast example uses 和 as a conjunction joining two nouns (苹果和饺子). As a preposition 和 means with and is followed by a verb phrase (我和朋友去); as a conjunction it joins two things into one unit (我喜欢苹果和饺子).

examples.reading: wǒ hé tā yìqǐ qù xuéxiào.
examples.translation: I go to school with him.
Mum is very kind to me.

examples.reading: wǒ hé jiějie zhù yí ge fángjiān.
examples.translation: I share a room with my older sister.
The teacher is very kind to us.

lessons.title: 和: joining words and phrases
lessons.summary: The conjunction 和 joins two nouns or phrases into one unit; it does not join sentences.
body: The conjunction 和 (hé, and) joins two nouns or phrases into one unit: 我和妹妹都喜欢猫, 我喜欢看书和写字. The joined unit acts as one subject or object.

The contrast example uses 和 as a preposition meaning with (我和朋友去电影院 = I go with friends). As a conjunction 和 joins two equal things; as a preposition it introduces a companion before a verb. 和 does not join two sentences (you cannot say 我去商店和我买书).

examples.reading: wǒ hé mèimei dōu xǐhuan māo.
examples.translation: My younger sister and I both like cats.

examples.text: 爸爸和妈妈都在公司工作。
examples.reading: bàba hé māma dōu zài gōngsī gōngzuò.
examples.translation: Dad and Mum both work at a company.

examples.reading: wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū hé xiě zì.

examples.text: 这本书和那本书都很好。
examples.reading: zhè běn shū hé nà běn shū dōu hěn hǎo.
examples.translation: This book and that book are both good.
I go to the cinema with a friend.

lessons.title: 的: linking a modifier to a noun
lessons.summary: 的 links an owner, adjective or clause to the noun it modifies.
body: 的 (de) links a modifier to a noun: possession (我的书), an adjective (大的苹果), or a clause (他写的字). With close people and groups it is often left out: 我妈妈, 我们学校.

The contrast example uses 得, which links a verb to a complement describing how the action is done (他说得很好). 的 goes before a noun; 得 goes after a verb. Do not use 的 to introduce a complement (说得好, not 说的很好).

examples.reading: tā xiě de zì hěn hǎokàn.
examples.translation: The characters he writes look nice.

lessons.title: 了: a completed action
lessons.summary: 了 after a verb marks that the action happened or is complete.
body: 了 (le) right after a verb marks a completed action: 我买了一本书, 他吃了三个饺子. To say it did not happen, use 没 and drop 了: 我没买.

The contrast example uses 过, which marks experience rather than a specific completed event (我没去过中国 = I have never been to China). After 没 use 过 for never (没去过), not 了 (you cannot say 没去了中国). 了 is for a specific finished action; 过 is for life experience.

examples.reading: wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū.
tā chī le sān ge jiǎozi.
wǒmen kàn le yí ge diànyǐng.
mèimei hē le yì bēi niúnǎi.
examples.translation: My younger sister drank a glass of milk.
I have never been to China.

lessons.title: Particles 吗 and 吧: questions and suggestions
lessons.summary: 吗 makes a yes-no question; 吧 makes a suggestion or a guess.
body: 吗 (ma) turns a statement into a yes-no question without changing the word order: 你是学生吗？ 吧 (ba) makes a suggestion (我们回家吧！= let us go home) or a guess (你是老师吧？= you are a teacher, right?).

The contrast example uses 呢, which cannot make a yes-no question. 呢 asks what about someone or something after a noun (我很好，你呢？= I am fine, and you?). Use 吗 for a yes-no question, 吧 for a suggestion or guess, 呢 for a follow-up.

lessons.title: Particles 了 and 呢: change and ongoing
lessons.summary: Sentence-final 了 announces a new situation; 呢 marks an ongoing action or softens a question.
body: At the end of a sentence 了 (le) announces that the situation has changed or come about: 下雨了 (it has started raining), 他会开车了 (he can drive now). 呢 (ne) marks an ongoing action (我吃饭呢 = I am eating) or softens a question with a question word (你在做什么呢？).

The contrast example uses 吗, which asks a yes-no question (你是医生吗？). 吗 does not combine with a question word or with 呢 (you cannot say 你在做什么吗？). Sentence-final 了 states a change; 呢 marks ongoing or a follow-up; 吗 asks yes-no.

lessons.title: 喂: hello on the phone
lessons.summary: 喂 is an interjection used to answer the phone or get someone's attention; it stands alone.
body: 喂 (wèi) is an interjection: it answers the phone or calls for attention (喂，你好！). It stands at the start, separated by a comma, and is not part of the sentence that follows.
The contrast example uses 请, which makes a polite request (请坐 = please sit). 喂 calls for attention; 请 asks someone politely to do something. Neither is a verb inside the sentence.

examples.translation: Hello, may I ask if he is in?
Hello, who are you looking for?

lessons.title: Basic phrase types: coordinate, modifier-head, verb-object, subject-predicate
lessons.summary: Phrases combine words: A和B, modifier+的+noun, verb+object, and subject+predicate.
body: Four basic phrase types: coordinate (我和妹妹, joined by 和), modifier-head (我的新书, a modifier before a noun), verb-object (看电影, a verb plus its object), and subject-predicate (他很好, a subject plus a predicate). Phrases combine into sentences.

The contrast example uses a preposition-object phrase (在家), which is an other type (next lesson): a preposition plus its object, used before a verb. The four basic types build the core of a sentence; preposition-object and place phrases modify it.

examples.translation: My younger sister and I go to school.

examples.reading: zhè shì wǒ de xīn shū.

examples.translation: I think he is very good.

lessons.title: Other phrase types: numeral-measure, preposition-object, place
lessons.summary: A numeral-measure phrase counts; a preposition-object phrase and a place phrase modify the verb.
body: Three other phrase types: numeral-measure (三本书, a number plus a measure word), preposition-object (在学校, 对我, a preposition plus its object), and place (桌子上, 家里, a noun plus a position word). They usually modify the verb or count a noun.
The contrast example uses a modifier-head phrase (我的书), a basic type: a modifier before a noun. A numeral-measure phrase counts a noun; a modifier-head phrase describes whose or which noun it is.

examples.translation: The book is on the table.

examples.reading: wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén.
examples.translation: There are five people in my family.

lessons.title: The subject: who or what the sentence is about
lessons.summary: A noun, pronoun or noun phrase can be the subject, before the predicate.
body: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. A noun (爸爸), a pronoun (我) or a noun phrase (我的老师, 这个商店) can be the subject. It comes before the predicate.
The contrast example uses the adverb 都, which is not part of the subject: it comes after the subject and before the verb (我们都喜欢他). Do not put 都 before the subject.

lessons.title: The predicate: what the subject does or is
lessons.summary: A verb, adjective or numeral-measure phrase can be the predicate; a noun predicate needs 是.
body: The predicate says what the subject does or is. A verb or verb phrase (吃米饭, 学习汉语), an adjective or adjective phrase (很冷), or a numeral-measure phrase (三岁) can be the predicate without 是.
The contrast example uses 是 for a noun predicate (他是医生). A noun cannot be the predicate on its own (you cannot say 他医生); it needs 是. An adjective does not take 是 (you cannot say 我是忙).

lessons.title: The object: what the action reaches
lessons.summary: A noun, pronoun or noun phrase can be the object, after the verb.
body: The object is what the action reaches. A noun (书), a pronoun (我) or a noun phrase (我的学校) can be the object. It comes after the verb: 看书, 认识我, 喜欢我的学校.
The contrast example uses a place phrase with 在, which comes before the verb, not as an object (我在家吃饭, not 我吃饭在家). Some verbs (睡觉, 上班) already contain their object and cannot take another.

lessons.title: The attributive: modifying a noun
lessons.summary: A noun word, adjective or numeral-measure phrase can modify a noun, often with 的.
body: The attributive modifies a noun: a noun word with 的 (我的书), an adjective (大苹果), or a numeral-measure phrase (两个姐姐). Some noun attributives drop 的 (汉语书, 我妈妈).
The contrast example uses 得, which introduces a complement after a verb (他汉语说得很好), not an attributive before a noun. 的 links a modifier to a noun; 得 links a verb to a complement.

examples.reading: tā Hànyǔ shuō de hěn hǎo.

lessons.title: The adverbial: modifying the verb
lessons.summary: An adverb, time word or place phrase can modify the verb, before it.
body: The adverbial modifies the verb or adjective: an adverb (很忙, 非常喜欢), a time word (明天去), or a place phrase (在家吃饭). It comes before the verb.

The contrast example uses 的, which links an attributive to a noun (我的书), not an adverbial to a verb. An adverbial modifies the action; an attributive modifies a thing. Do not put the time or place after the verb.

lessons.title: Action-measure complement: counting an action
lessons.summary: 一下 (and 一次) after a verb counts how many times the action happens.
body: An action-measure complement counts occurrences of an action: 看一下, 问了一下. 一下 means once, a short try; 了 goes between the verb and 一下 (我看了一下). 一次 also means one time.
The contrast example uses 一点儿, which measures a quantity of a thing (喝一点儿水), not occurrences of an action. 一下 counts the action; 一点儿 measures the thing.

examples.reading: wǒ qù le yí cì yīyuàn.
examples.translation: I went to the hospital once.

lessons.title: Simple sentences: four predicate types
lessons.summary: A simple sentence has a verb, adjective, noun or no-subject predicate.
body: Four simple-sentence types by predicate: verb-predicate (他喜欢狗), adjective-predicate (今天天气很好), noun-predicate (今天星期三 — no 是 needed for dates and age), and non-subject-predicate (下雨了 — no subject).
The contrast example uses 是 for an identity sentence (我是学生). A noun-predicate sentence about date or age needs no 是; an identity or category sentence does need 是.

lessons.title: Declarative sentences: stating a fact
lessons.summary: A declarative states a fact with normal word order and ends in a period.
body: A declarative sentence states a fact: 我是学生, 他喜欢喝茶, 今天不冷. The word order is subject then predicate, and it ends in a period (。).

The contrast example uses 吗, which turns the same statement into a yes-no question (你是学生吗？) ending in a question mark. Adding 吗 changes a fact into a question; do not add it to a sentence you mean as a statement.

examples.translation: I do not have a younger brother.

lessons.title: Question types: yes-no, wh-, affirmative-negative
lessons.summary: Ask with 吗 (yes-no), a question word (wh-), or verb-not-verb (affirmative-negative).
body: Three question types: yes-no with 吗 (你是老师吗？), wh- with a question word in the answer position (你叫什么名字？, 这是谁的书？), and affirmative-negative with verb-not-verb (你去不去学校？). The affirmative-negative form does not take 吗.

The contrast example uses 呢 for a follow-up question (我很好，你呢？= and you?). 呢 asks what about someone; it is not a yes-no, wh- or affirmative-negative question. Do not add 吗 to a wh- or affirmative-negative question.

lessons.title: Imperative sentences: requests and commands
lessons.summary: 请 + verb makes a polite request; 不要 + verb forbids; the subject is often omitted.
body: An imperative gives a command or request. 请 (qǐng, please) makes it polite: 请坐, 请喝茶. 不要 (bú yào, do not) forbids: 不要说话, 不要看电视. The subject is usually left out.
The contrast example uses 吧, which softens a command into a suggestion (我们回家吧！= let us go home). 请 and 不要 address the listener directly; 吧 proposes doing something together.

lessons.title: Exclamative sentences: strong feeling
lessons.summary: 太…了！, 真…！ and 好…！ express strong feeling and end in an exclamation mark.
body: An exclamative expresses strong feeling: 太 + adjective + 了 (太好了！, 太贵了！), 真 + adjective (真漂亮！), or 好 + adjective (好大的苹果！). It ends in an exclamation mark (！).
The contrast example uses 很 in a plain statement (今天很热。), which just describes without strong feeling. 太 usually needs 了 to exclaim; a bare 太贵 is incomplete. 很 states a degree; 太 and 真 exclaim.

lessons.title: 是: A is B (identity or category)
lessons.summary: 是 links two nouns to say A is B; its negative is 不是.
body: 是 (shì) links two nouns to say A is B, an identity or category: 我是学生, 他是医生, 这是我的书. To negate, put 不 before it: 不是 (bú shì).
The contrast example uses 很 with an adjective (今天很冷). An adjective is a predicate on its own and does not take 是 (you cannot say 我是忙); 是 is for linking nouns, 很 is for describing with an adjective.

lessons.title: 有: possession
lessons.summary: 有 says someone has something; its negative is 没有, never 不有.
body: 有 (yǒu) says someone has something: 我有一个哥哥, 她有两只猫. Its negative is 没有 (méiyǒu), never 不有.
The contrast example uses 是 for identity (他是学生 = he is a student). 有 says what someone has (我有书); 是 says what someone or something is (这是书). Do not use 是 for possession or 有 for identity.

examples.translation: He does not have a car.

examples.reading: wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén.
examples.translation: There are five people in my family.

lessons.title: Existential sentences: what is at a place
lessons.summary: Place + 是 + noun identifies; place + 有 + numeral-measure + noun says what exists there.
body: An existential sentence introduces what is at a place. Place + 是 + noun identifies it (前边是一个书店); place + 有 + numeral-measure + noun says what exists there (桌子上有三本书).

The contrast example uses 在 with the thing first (书在桌子上), which says where the book is. An existential sentence puts the place first and introduces the thing; a 在 sentence puts the thing first and gives its place.

examples.reading: xuéxiào li yǒu yí ge lǎoshī.
examples.translation: There is a teacher in the school.

examples.reading: zhuōzi shàng yǒu sān běn shū.
examples.translation: There are three books on the table.

examples.reading: xuéxiào wàibian yǒu yí ge shāngdiàn.
examples.translation: There is a shop outside the school.
The book is on the table.

lessons.title: Serial-verb sentences: purpose or manner
lessons.summary: Two verbs share one subject: the second is the purpose of the first, or the first is the manner of the second.
body: In a serial-verb sentence two verbs share one subject and happen in order. The second action is the purpose of the first (我去商店买书 = I go to the shop to buy books); or the first is the manner of the second (他坐出租车去学校 = he goes to school by taxi).

The contrast example uses the preposition 和 (我和朋友去书店 = I go with a friend), which introduces a companion, not a second action. A serial-verb sentence has two actions by one subject; a 和 phrase has one action with a companion.

examples.translation: I go to the shop to buy books.
He goes to school by taxi.
Mum goes to the hospital to see a doctor.
I go to the bookshop with a friend.

lessons.title: Double-object sentences: verb + person + thing
lessons.summary: Some verbs take two objects: a person first, then a thing (给我一本书).
body: Some verbs take two objects: a person (the receiver) first, then a thing (what is given or asked). 给 (gěi, give): 我给你一本书. 问 (wèn, ask): 老师问我问题. The person comes before the thing.

The contrast example uses the preposition 对 (妈妈对我很好), which introduces the target of an attitude, not a transferred thing. A double-object verb transfers or asks something; 对 just points to whom an attitude is directed.

examples.reading: wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.
wǒ wèn nǐ yí jiàn shì.

examples.translation: Mum is very kind to me.

lessons.title: Coordinate clauses: …也…, …还…
lessons.summary: Two statements are joined by a comma with 也 or 还 in the second; no conjunction is needed.
body: A coordinate complex sentence joins two equal statements with a comma and 也 (also) or 还 (more) in the second: 我喜欢看书，也喜欢看电影; 他会说汉语，还会写汉字. No conjunction like and is needed.
The contrast example uses 和 to join two words inside one clause (我和妹妹都喜欢猫). 也 / 还 join two clauses; 和 joins words or phrases within one clause. Do not use 和 to join two sentences.

examples.text: 我喜欢看书，也喜欢看电影。
examples.reading: wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū, yě xǐhuan kàn diànyǐng.
examples.translation: I like reading, and I also like watching films.

examples.text: 他会说汉语，还会写汉字。
examples.reading: tā huì shuō Hànyǔ, hái huì xiě Hànzì.
examples.translation: He can speak Chinese, and he can also write characters.

examples.reading: jīntiān hěn lěng, hái xià yǔ.
examples.translation: It is cold today, and it is also raining.

examples.reading: wǒ shì xuéshēng, tā yě shì xuéshēng.
examples.translation: I am a student, and he is a student too.

examples.reading: wǒ hé mèimei dōu xǐhuan māo.
examples.translation: My younger sister and I both like cats.

lessons.title: Completed aspect: 了1
lessons.summary: 了1 right after the verb marks a completed action; negate with 没 and drop 了.
body: 了1 (le) right after the verb marks the action as completed: 我吃了饭, 他写了一个字. It is about the action finishing, not about a change of situation.
The contrast example shows the negative: 我没吃饭. To say a completed action did not happen, use 没 and drop 了 (you cannot say 没吃了饭). 不 is for habits or the future, not for a past completed action.

examples.reading: tā xiě le yí ge zì.
wǒmen hē le yì bēi chá.
examples.translation: We drank a cup of tea.

examples.reading: mèimei chuān le yí jiàn xīn yīfu.
examples.translation: My younger sister put on a new piece of clothing.

lessons.title: Change aspect: 了2
lessons.summary: Sentence-final 了2 marks a new situation or a change: it is so now.
body: 了2 (le) at the end of a sentence marks a new situation or change: 天冷了 (it has got cold), 我会说汉语了 (I can speak Chinese now), 他不去学校了 (he is not going to school anymore). It is about the situation now, not about one finished action.

The contrast example uses 了1 right after the verb (我买了一个苹果), which marks a completed action. 了1 follows the verb and marks completion; 了2 ends the sentence and marks change. Both can appear together, but they do different jobs.

examples.translation: He is not going to school anymore.

examples.reading: wǒ mǎi le yí ge píngguǒ.

lessons.title: Progressive aspect: 在/正在…呢
lessons.summary: 在/正在 before the verb, or 呢 at the end, marks an action in progress.
body: The progressive marks an action in progress: 在 / 正在 before the verb (我在看书, 爸爸正在打电话), 呢 at the end (他吃饭呢), or both (妹妹在睡觉呢).

The contrast example uses 了1 (我吃了饭), which marks a completed action. The progressive says the action is happening now; 了 says it is finished. They mark different aspects and are not used for the same meaning.

lessons.title: Number expressions: money and ordinals
lessons.summary: Money is number + 块 (spoken) or 元 (formal); ordinals are 第 + number.
body: Money: number + 块 (kuài, spoken) or 元 (yuán, formal): 二十块, 一千元. Ordinals: 第 + number: 第一 (first), 第二 (second). 第 makes an order, not a count.
The contrast example uses 两 before a measure word (我有两个哥哥). Before a measure word, two is 两, not 二; 第 + number is an ordinal, while a bare number counts.

examples.translation: This phone is a thousand yuan.

examples.reading: zhè shì wǒ de dì-yī běn shū.

examples.translation: A cup of tea is ten yuan.

lessons.title: Time expressions: dates, weekdays and clock time
lessons.summary: Dates run year-month-day, weekdays are 星期 + number, and clock time is number + 点 + 分.
body: Dates run from big to small: year + 月 + 日 / 号 (三月五号). Weekdays are 星期 + number (星期一 to 星期六, 星期日 / 星期天). Clock time is number + 点 + number + 分 (八点十分). 号 is spoken, 日 is written.
The contrast example uses 半 (half): 现在两点半 (it is half past two). 半 marks the half hour; 分 marks minutes. Both come after 点.

examples.translation: I am going to China next year.
He has class in the morning.
